what it says: circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law a Pharisee
an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin
a Hebrew, an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham
"Saul of Tarsus"; a Jew of Tarsus in Cilicia, "a citizen of no mean city"; born at Tarsus. The letters never name his home town
"I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees"; lived as a Pharisee, the strictest party
always "Paul"; the name Saul never appears in any letter
called Saul until Acts 13:9, "Saul, who is also called Paul", and Paul from then on; the risen Jesus calls him "Saoul" in Hebrew form (Ac 9:4)
"three times I was beaten with rods", a punishment given by Roman magistrates; the letters never say he was a Roman citizen

a Roman citizen by birth; protests that citizens were beaten uncondemned at Philippi; appeals to Caesar. In tension with 2 Cor 11:25 (three beatings with rods), though citizens were sometimes beaten illegally
advanced in Judaism beyond many of his own age, extremely zealous for the traditions of his fathers
brought up in Jerusalem, educated "at the feet of Gamaliel"; lived from youth among his own nation in Jerusalem
worked night and day with his own hands so as not to burden anyone; refused his right to be supported
a tentmaker (skenopoios) by trade, working with Aquila and Priscilla; "these hands ministered to my needs"
worked night and day so as not to burden them, to give an example
persecuted the church of God violently and tried to destroy it
"I was still unknown by face to the churches of Judea"; they only heard "the one who once persecuted us now preaches the faith"

ravaged the church in Jerusalem, dragging men and women to prison; got letters from the high priest to arrest believers in the synagogues of Damascus; voted for their deaths. Hard to square with Ga 1:22 (unknown by face in Judea), though not impossible
present at the stoning of Stephen, guarding the witnesses' cloaks, approving of his death
formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor and a man of violence
God "revealed his Son in me"; "have I not seen Jesus our Lord?"; "last of all he appeared also to me"; afterwards he "returned to Damascus", so the call was near it

a light and a voice on the road to Damascus; blinded three days; healed and baptized by Ananias. Acts' three tellings differ among themselves (his companions hear the voice in 9:7, do not hear it in 22:9)
the risen Jesus foretells that a persecutor, Saul, will be called and will preach to the gentiles
"I did not confer with flesh and blood, nor go up to Jerusalem ... but I went away into Arabia, and returned again to Damascus"
preaches in the synagogues of Damascus "immediately", then "after many days" escapes; Acts has no journey to Arabia
the ethnarch of King Aretas guarded the city of Damascus to seize him; he was let down in a basket through a window in the wall
"the Jews" plotted to kill him and watched the gates; the disciples let him down over the wall in a basket. Same escape, different pursuers; Aretas is not named

Aretas IV ruled the Nabataeans c. 9 BCE - 40 CE (his coins are dated by regnal year); Josephus tells of his war with Herod Antipas c. 36. Nabataean authority in Damascus in the 30s is not attested outside 2 Corinthians and is debated

episode title: First visit to Jerusalem as a believer
what it says: after three years went up to Jerusalem to visit Cephas and stayed fifteen days; saw no other apostle except James the Lord's brother; "before God, I do not lie"

episode title: First visit to Jerusalem as a believer
what it says: the disciples fear him; Barnabas brings him "to the apostles"; he goes in and out among them in Jerusalem, preaching boldly, until Hellenists try to kill him. Galatians swears he saw only Cephas and James and stayed unknown by face to the churches of Judea

episode title: First visit to Jerusalem as a believer
what it says: in a trance in the Temple the Lord tells him to leave Jerusalem quickly and go to the gentiles
then went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia
sent to Tarsus; later Barnabas fetches him to Antioch, where they teach for a year and the disciples are first called "Christians"
"then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem", the next visit in a sworn list (Ga 1:20) of his contacts with Jerusalem

Barnabas and Saul take famine relief from Antioch to the elders in Judea. An extra visit between Ga 1:18 and Ga 2:1 contradicts Galatians, unless Galatians 2 is this visit (as some scholars hold), in which case Acts 15 becomes the problem
a severe famine in Judea under the governor Tiberius Alexander (c. 46-48), relieved by Queen Helena of Adiabene; matches the famine "under Claudius" of Ac 11:28

episode title: First journey: Cyprus and southern Asia Minor
where: Cyprus, Perge, Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, Derbe
what it says: John Mark leaves them at Perge; synagogue sermon at Pisidian Antioch; Iconium; at Lystra a lame man is healed and the crowd hails Barnabas as Zeus and Paul as Hermes

episode title: First journey: Cyprus and southern Asia Minor
where: Cyprus, Perge, Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, Derbe
what it says: "once I was stoned"

episode title: First journey: Cyprus and southern Asia Minor

went up "by revelation" with Barnabas and Titus; laid out his gospel privately to "those of repute"; Titus not compelled to be circumcised; "false brothers" spied on their freedom; James, Cephas and John gave the right hand of fellowship and "added nothing" to him, asking only that he remember the poor
on food offered to idols, argues from knowledge and conscience: "eat whatever is sold in the market"; never cites any ruling from Jerusalem

people: Barnabas, Peter, James, Judas Barsabbas, Silas

Paul says they "added nothing" to him (Ga 2:6) and never cites the decree on idol food; Titus is absent from Acts
years later James tells Paul about the decree as if it were news to him

episode title: The Antioch incident and the split with Barnabas
what it says: at Antioch Cephas ate with gentiles until "certain men came from James", then withdrew; even Barnabas was carried away; Paul opposed Cephas "to his face"

episode title: The Antioch incident and the split with Barnabas
what it says: Paul and Barnabas part over whether to take John Mark; Acts has no clash with Peter

(Ga 5:11); Timothy, with a Jewish mother, may be a different case
Timothy his "true child in the faith"; his mother Eunice and grandmother Lois were believers
Silvanus co-sends 1 Thessalonians and preached at Corinth with Paul and Timothy
Silas travels with Paul, is jailed with him at Philippi and rejoins him at Corinth
a vision of a man of Macedonia calling for help; the first "we" passage begins
"we had already suffered and been shamefully treated at Philippi"; the Philippians alone shared with him in giving and sent help to Thessalonica more than once
the church has overseers and deacons; Euodia and Syntyche "laboured side by side with me in the gospel"; a "true yokefellow"; Clement
Lydia the purple-seller is baptized; a slave girl exorcized; Paul and Silas beaten with rods and jailed; earthquake; the jailer converts; Paul claims citizenship
"the blessed and glorious Paul, when he was among you ... taught accurately ... and when absent wrote you letters"; he laboured among them
the Thessalonians "turned to God from idols" (gentiles); he worked night and day there; they suffered from their own countrymen; "Satan hindered us" from returning

three sabbaths in the synagogue; converts are Jews, devout Greeks and leading women; the mob attacks Jason's house; flight to Beroea. Acts implies a few weeks; Philippians says help was sent to him there more than once (Php 4:16)
the city's magistrates are called "politarchs" in its inscriptions, the title Acts uses (Ac 17:6, 8)

Silas and Timothy stay in Beroea while Paul waits alone at Athens; they rejoin him only at Corinth. In 1 Thessalonians Timothy was with him at Athens and was sent back
debates with Epicureans and Stoics; the Areopagus speech on the "unknown god"; a few believe
came "in weakness and in fear and much trembling"; baptized Crispus, Gaius and the household of Stephanas, "the first fruits of Achaia"; took no money from them, supplied by brothers from Macedonia

from Corinth: Gaius is host to Paul and the whole church; "Erastus the city treasurer" sends greetings

reference: Fouilles de Delphes III 4:286; SIG3 801 D

Claudius "expelled from Rome the Jews, who were constantly rioting at the instigation of Chrestus"; Orosius (5th century, 7.6.15) dates it to 49
"Erastus, in return for his aedileship, laid [this pavement] at his own expense"; both its date and whether he is the "city treasurer" of Ro 16:23 are disputed
factions "I belong to Paul", "I belong to Apollos"; "I planted, Apollos watered"; Apollos unwilling to come now
Apollos, an eloquent Alexandrian Jew, taught by Priscilla and Aquila at Ephesus, goes on to Corinth
"speed Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way"
Paul wrote to the Corinthians "about himself and Cephas and Apollos, because even then you had made factions"

staying at Ephesus until Pentecost, "a wide door ... and many adversaries"; "I fought with beasts at Ephesus"; an affliction in Asia so severe "we despaired of life itself ... we had received the sentence of death"

two years and more at Ephesus, teaching in the hall of Tyrannus; healing handkerchiefs; the sons of Sceva; magic books burned; the riot of Demetrius the silversmith, from which Paul is kept away. Acts has no imprisonment or mortal danger for Paul at Ephesus
farewell speech to the Ephesian elders at Miletus: "you will not see my face again"
the cult of Artemis, silversmiths' guilds, the great theatre and the provincial "Asiarchs" (Ac 19:31) are all attested at Ephesus
Paul is thrown to a lion in the stadium; the lion, which Paul had baptized, will not harm him: a literal reading of "I fought with beasts at Ephesus"

"in prisons far more" than his rivals (written before the arrest in Acts 21); his chains are known "throughout the whole praetorium"; "those of Caesar's household" greet; a prisoner with Epaphras; Andronicus and Junia "my fellow prisoners"
one night in prison at Philippi before his last arrest, then custody in Jerusalem, Caesarea and Rome; none of the earlier imprisonments of 2 Cor 11:23
"seven times he bore chains, was exiled, was stoned"
"remember my chains"; "the prisoner of Christ Jesus"; "an ambassador in chains"

people: Tychicus, Onesimus, Aristarchus, Mark, Epaphras, Luke, Demas, Archippus

rival teachers preach "another gospel"; "false brothers"; "super-apostles", "false apostles"; "beware of the dogs"; some slander him as saying "let us do evil that good may come"
men from Judea and believing Pharisees demand circumcision; thousands of believing Jews "zealous for the law" have heard that he teaches Jews to abandon Moses
the Ebionites "repudiate the apostle Paul, calling him an apostate from the law"
his letters contain things "hard to understand, which the ignorant and unstable twist"
a collection from Galatia, Macedonia and Achaia for "the poor among the saints at Jerusalem"; chosen delegates to carry it; fear that it may not be acceptable and of "the unbelievers in Judea"

"after several years I came to bring alms to my nation": Acts' only mention of the collection

going to Jerusalem; asks for prayer to be "rescued from the unbelievers in Judea"
Troas (Eutychus raised), Miletus, Tyre, Caesarea; Agabus foretells his arrest; a "we" passage
James and the elders ask him to pay for four men's Nazirite vows in the Temple, to show he keeps the law (compare 1 Cor 9:20, "to the Jews I became as a Jew")
Jews from Asia accuse him of bringing Trophimus the Ephesian into the Temple; a mob; the tribune rescues him
notices on the Temple barrier forbade gentiles to pass on pain of death; two have been found (1871, 1935)
the tribune asks "are you not the Egyptian who stirred up a revolt and led 4,000 men of the sicarii into the wilderness?"
an Egyptian false prophet under Felix led a crowd (30,000 in War) to the Mount of Olives and escaped; the numbers differ from Acts
the high priest Ananias orders him struck; "God is going to strike you, you whitewashed wall"
Ananias son of Nedebaeus, high priest c. 47-59
sent to the governor Felix at Caesarea; prosecuted by Tertullus; Felix and his Jewish wife Drusilla hear him; Felix hopes for a bribe and holds him two years
Felix, a freedman, governor of Judea c. 52-60, married Drusilla, sister of Agrippa II
Festus succeeds Felix; Paul appeals to Caesar; King Agrippa and Bernice hear him: "this man could have been set free if he had not appealed"
Porcius Festus, governor c. 60-62, died in office; Agrippa II and his sister Bernice (also Tacitus, Histories 2.2)
"three times I was shipwrecked; a night and a day I spent in the open sea", all before the Rome voyage of Acts

sails under the centurion Julius of the Augustan cohort; storm; shipwreck on Malta; a viper; heals the father of Publius, "the chief man of the island". Acts reports none of the three earlier shipwrecks

reference: CIG 5754 and other inscriptions of Malta and Gozo
what it says: "first" (protos) is attested as an official title in the Maltese islands
his imprisonment has become known "throughout the whole praetorium"; "those of Caesar's household" greet (Rome, if Philippians was written there)
met by believers at the Forum of Appius; two years in rented lodging under guard, preaching "unhindered"; Acts ends without his trial or death
Onesiphorus searched for him in Rome; at his first defence no one stood by him; "rescued from the lion's mouth"
Peter and Paul preached at Rome and founded the church there, then handed the office of bishop to Linus. Romans is written to an established church Paul has never visited (Ro 1:10-13; Ro 15:20-23)
Peter and Paul both planted the church at Corinth and taught together in Italy. In 1 Corinthians Paul planted it and Apollos watered (1Co 3:6)
may live or die; "even if I am to be poured out as a drink-offering"; the letters record no death
tells the Ephesian elders they will not see his face again; ends with him alive and preaching in Rome
"I am already being poured out ... the time of my departure has come; I have finished the race"
"he bore witness before the rulers, and so departed from the world"
the Ephesians are "fellow initiates with Paul ... in whose footsteps may I be found when I reach God" (Ignatius on his own way to martyrdom)
Peter and Paul were martyred at the same time in Italy
"I can show you the trophies of the apostles: on the Vatican and on the Ostian Way"
at Rome "Paul is crowned with a death like John's" (beheading)
Nero has Paul beheaded; milk spurts from his neck; he appears to Nero afterwards
"his bodily presence is weak, and his speech of no account"; "unskilled in speech"; a "thorn in the flesh"; ill when he first came to Galatia; "see with what large letters I write with my own hand"

the chief speaker, hailed as Hermes; a polished orator at the Areopagus; "your great learning is driving you mad". Acts' eloquent Paul against the letters' "unskilled in speech" (which may be modesty)
"a man small in size, bald-headed, bow-legged, well built, with eyebrows meeting and a rather long nose, full of grace": the only physical description
caught up to the third heaven and into paradise fourteen years before; went to Jerusalem "by revelation"; "the signs of an apostle ... signs and wonders and mighty works"
blinds a magician; heals a lame man; visions; an exorcism; handkerchiefs that heal; raises Eutychus; survives a viper; heals the sick on Malta

"I wish that all were as I myself am"; good for the unmarried "to remain as I am"; he has the right to take along a believing wife "as the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas", but does not
Paul had a wife, the "yokefellow" of Php 4:3, but did not take her about with him
Paul preaches "blessed are the continent"; Thecla breaks off her engagement to Thamyris. The letters allow marriage (1Co 7:2, 9, 28)
signs greetings "with my own hand"; "I Tertius, who wrote this letter"; an earlier letter to Corinth; "his letters are weighty and strong"
warns of a letter "as if from us"; his signature is "the sign in every letter"; a letter "from Laodicea"
Acts never mentions Paul writing letters; the only letter in Acts is the council's
Paul wrote to the Corinthians about himself, Cephas and Apollos
Paul mentions the Ephesians "in every letter"
Paul, when absent, "wrote you letters"
"in all his letters", set beside "the other scriptures"

Paul wrote to seven churches, and to Philemon, Titus and twice to Timothy; letters to the Laodiceans and the Alexandrians were forged in his name for Marcion's sect
"Luke, my fellow worker"
"Luke the beloved physician"; "only Luke is with me"
the "we" passages: the narrator travels with Paul (a real companion, a source, or a literary device; debated)
Luke, a follower of Paul, wrote down the gospel Paul preached and was "inseparable" from him
a Cephas party at Corinth; Cephas travels with his wife; the risen Jesus appeared first to Cephas
Peter last appears at the council, on Paul's side; Acts never tells of the Antioch clash (Ga 2:11-14)
Peter and Paul as the two great martyr apostles of "our own generation". The letters show partners who quarrelled
"I do not command you as Peter and Paul did: they were apostles, I am a convict"

Priscilla and Aquila; Jason of Thessalonica; Sopater of Beroea; Gaius
"greet Prisca and Aquila and the household of Onesiphorus"
"I have no one like him ... they all seek their own interests"
